newsitem.title: USA: NASA astronaut says he not sure about Mir repairs.
newsitem.headline: NASA astronaut says he not sure about Mir repairs.

text.p: The NASA astronaut aboard the troubled Russian space station Mir said on Wednesday he was not sure if it would be possible to repressurize the Spektr module, damaged by a supply ship in a near-fatal crash last month.

U.S. physicist Michael Foale, in an interview on a pool basis with CBS journalist Bill Harwood from the Kennedy Space Centre in Cape Canaveral, Florida, said repairs would depend on the extent of damage to the 40-foot (12 metre) Spektr module, which was struck by a resupply ship on June 25.
"The whole plan as it's laid out to us looks good," Foale said during the 20-minute video linkup. "However, we do not know whether it will work, as far as repressurizing Spektr goes."
The collision forced the Mir crew to seal off the Spektr module, where Foale slept and scientific experiments were performed.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev said on Wednesday the crash could have killed the two Russians and one American on board.
"If it had hit us directly, it would have punctured the core module directly and we would have all died," Tsibliyev said through a NASA translator.

"Until the very end I was holding the handles to try and get the craft not to hit the station," he said. "If I had not been doing that I am sure that it would have hit the station directly. If it had done so, we would have either died or we would have just been metal floating in space."
British-born Foale said problems with the Mir space station, a collection of modules attached to a core station, should not dissuade the United States from continuing joint missions with Russia.

"This experience is really, really valuable for us now," he said. "I don't think it's a great price to pay for the U.S. to have the permanent presence of an astronaut on board the Russian space station Mir."
Foale said finding "new solutions" to problems on the 11-year-old Mir offered valuable lessons that would be useful in the future.
"Those lessons we will only come across ourselves on the international space station in a few years from now, once it's been established in space," he said.

Foale will stay on board until an American shuttle arrives on Sept. 20. On Wednesday, he wished his wife a happy 10th wedding anniversary. "We've had 10 great years and I hope my 30th anniversary will be with her on the surface of Mars," he said.
Foale, who will be replaced by NASA astronaut Wendy Lawrence, a U.S. Navy commander, said morale has not suffered because of serious problems on the space station.

"Bad things happened here. We never got depressed or demoralised by this. We just worked through these problems," he said. "We just approach those steadily, progressively, day by day and do the best we can to put them right."
When asked, Foale did not say who accidently unplugged a vital computer, causing the station to lose its orientation for more than a day.
"The crew were unplugging one of about 100 or so cables and they're big, big thick cables and they're all the same colour. They all look the same," he said. "One of those was mistakenly unplugged."
The two Russian cosmonauts who came aboard Mir on Feb. 12 are scheduled to return to Earth on Aug. 14.
